title: Set the Night on Fire: L.A. in the Sixties
author: Mike Davis
Jon Wiener
target_audience: Students and scholars of social movements
General audiences seeking insight into 1960s Los Angeles
Fans of Mike Davis, Jon Wiener, or radical history
core_themes: Intersections of race, class, and power
The struggle over city space and police brutality
primary_purpose: To provide a comprehensive and nuanced account of Los Angeles as a center of radical activism and transformation during the 1960s, highlighting overlooked social movements, unsung heroes, and the city’s role as a crucible for protest and change.

structure_format.organization: Organized thematically and chronologically; each chapter focuses on particular communities, movements, or pivotal incidents
features: Detailed archival research and oral histories
Maps and photographs for historical context
Appendices with key resources and further reading

key_concepts_lessons: Los Angeles was a major epicenter of 1960s radicalism, not merely a backdrop.
The civil rights and Chicano movements, antiwar protests, gay liberation, and feminist activism all converged in the city.
Grassroots coalitions often formed across Black, Latinx, Asian American, and white working class groups.
State violence and police repression played pivotal roles in shaping LA’s social conflicts.
Major events—such as the Watts Uprising and high school walkouts—were products of long histories of local organizing.
Stories of marginalized activists are central to understanding broader American social changes.
style_tone: Nuanced, giving voice to multiple communities
notable_features: Emphasis on marginalized and grassroots actors, not only celebrity figures
Integration of firsthand interviews and new archival findings
Challenges dominant cultural narratives about LA as apolitical or only “glamorous”
Holistic approach to interwoven struggles—racial, economic, sexual, and generational
cultural_historical_context: Published in 2020 against the backdrop of renewed racial justice movements, the book revisits 1960s Los Angeles to illuminate underappreciated stories of resistance and suggest parallels to contemporary activism and urban struggles.
reception_impact: Critically acclaimed for its depth, detail, and fresh perspective on the Sixties
Praised for its inclusivity, bringing forward lesser-known voices and movements
Sparked discussions about how history informs ongoing struggles for justice in LA and America
Seen as a new standard resource for understanding urban radicalism
